script.opening: (Friendly, a bit embarrassed, then pleading.) "So I had a seizure last week — first one in ages. I'll be honest, I'd been missing my tablets, just got busy and ran out, and I felt fine so I didn't rush to sort it. I'm back on them now, though. I can carry on driving, can't I? I drive for my job — I can't manage without my car. Please don't tell me I have to stop."

facts.text: "At home. It was like my usual ones. I felt rough after, but I didn't hurt myself as far as I know." Partner saw it: stiffening and jerking for about 2 minutes, bit his tongue, confused for 20 minutes. Didn't go to hospital.

"Running out, mostly. I kept meaning to order the repeat. And yeah, I felt fine, so it didn't seem urgent." Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily — missed about 5 days. Restarted 6 days ago at full dose (if asked: didn't check with anyone how to restart).

"Work's been full on. Long days. That's partly why I let the tablets slide." Sleeping 5–6 hours. If asked: "Not that I noticed" — no illness, no new medicines, not drinking more than usual (a few beers at weekends).
Diagnosed at 19 (generalised tonic-clonic seizures). Last seizure 4 years ago. Sees the epilepsy nurse rarely. No rash or side-effects from lamotrigine. No allergies.
Group 1 car licence only. Sales rep covering the region; drives 300 miles a week. Hasn't driven since the seizure "except to the shop".
"Worried, if I'm honest. Mainly about work." No low mood or thoughts of self-harm.
Lives with partner, Mai, who doesn't drive. Mortgage. Bus to work is possible but slow.

Hoping for a yes: "If I can't drive, I don't know how I keep my job. I've got bills. That's why I'm hoping you'll say restarting the tablets sorts it." When told he must stop: "(silence) …For how long?" then "A year. That's… a lot." Tests the doctor: "And if I just… kept quiet?" — then, if the doctor is honest and kind: "No, I get it. I don't want to hurt anyone." Interested in practical help (pharmacy repeat, alarms, Access to Work).

ice.ideas: "I'm back on the tablets, so I'm safe to drive."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — losing his job and income if he can't drive; embarrassed about letting his tablets lapse.
ice.expectations: "To be told I can keep driving."

cues: "Please don't tell me I have to stop." — he half-knows the answer.
"I ran out." — adherence barriers to solve.
"And if I just… kept quiet?" — the doctor's duty to explain.

checkpoints.text: Explores WHY the medication was missed (busy/forgot, ran out/supply, beliefs, side-effects, cost, routine) non-judgementally and reinforces consistent adherence and the danger of abrupt stopping
Reviews seizure control/type/triggers and this seizure’s features/injury, considers neurology review/optimisation, and screens mood and (sensitively) SUDEP/safety awareness
States the DVLA DUTY clearly — after a seizure he MUST STOP DRIVING and notify the DVLA, and cannot continue simply because he has restarted medication

Knows the driving rules — Group 1: 12 months free of any seizure for established epilepsy (the 6-month first-seizure period does not apply to him; the medication-change route applies only to changes made on medical advice); Group 2: 10 years seizure-free without medication (DVLA, November 2025 edition) — and frames that meeting the criteria allows relicensing

Understands the DOCTOR’S professional duty: advise clearly, document, and — per GMC — if the patient continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded, make every effort and then contact the DVLA medical adviser promptly (telling the patient first and confirming in writing afterwards; GMC 2017)
Empathises with the livelihood impact and handles the non-adherence supportively (not blaming), while being clear and honest about the driving duty WITHOUT colluding with "I can keep driving"
Explains the rules and reasoning so he understands, frames regaining control as the route back to driving, signposts work/practical support, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: documents the driving advice, supports adherence (reminders/supply), arranges neurology review as needed, seizure-safety advice, fit note/Access to Work signposting, and review — honest DVLA duty handled supportively, not colluding with continued driving

worked.txt: "Thanks for being honest about missing the tablets — that’s really useful, and it’s common when life gets busy. The key thing is they only work taken regularly, and stopping suddenly can actually trigger seizures. Let’s sort out a system so you don’t run out — reminders, repeat prescriptions, pharmacy ordering."

"Tell me about the seizure — were you hurt, how long, anything else going on like lack of sleep or alcohol? And how’s your mood with all this? I may ask the neurologist to review your medication too."

"Now I have to be straight with you, and I know it’s the bit you didn’t want to hear. After a seizure, the law says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA — restarting your tablets doesn’t change that. I’m really sorry, because I know your job depends on it."

"It’s not necessarily forever. For a car licence, with epilepsy the DVLA rule is that you need to be free of any seizure for 12 months from last week’s, and then you can apply to be relicensed — the DVLA makes that decision. Getting back on top of your medication is exactly what gets you driving again."

"To be clear: it’s your legal responsibility to notify the DVLA and not drive in the meantime. I’ll document that I’ve advised you. I have to be honest that if someone keeps driving against this advice, I would have to inform the DVLA myself — I’d tell you first and confirm it to you in writing — but I’d much rather support you to do the right thing."

"Let’s think about work — a fit note suggesting amended duties if there’s non-driving work you can do, talking to your employer, and Access to Work, which can help pay for travel to work when you can’t drive. Avoid heights, swimming alone, and risky tasks until things are stable. I’ll review you, support the medication, and we’ll get you back to driving the proper way."

f.learning: A breakthrough seizure after missed medication is both a clinical and a professional consultation. Clinically, explore WHY the medication was missed (busy/forgot, ran out/supply problems, beliefs such as "felt fine", side-effects, cost, chaotic routine) non-judgementally, reinforce that anti-seizure medication must be taken consistently and that abruptly stopping can precipitate seizures (rarely status), and problem-solve adherence (reminders, repeat prescriptions, pharmacy ordering); review seizure type/control/triggers and any injury, consider neurology review/optimisation, and sensitively screen mood and SUDEP/safety awareness. The critical professional/safety duty is DRIVING: after a seizure there is a LEGAL obligation to inform the DVLA and the patient MUST STOP DRIVING — restarting tablets does not change this. The broad rules: Group 1 (car/motorcycle) generally requires a seizure-free period before relicensing (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025 edition: 12 months free of any seizure for established epilepsy — the 6-month period applies only after a first unprovoked seizure, and the medication-change route only when the change was on medical advice), while Group 2 (HGV/bus) requires 10 years seizure-free without medication; the exact period is set by DVLA criteria, but the immediate message is stop now and notify, framing that good control and meeting the criteria are the route back to driving. The doctor’s duty is to ADVISE this clearly, explain why, and DOCUMENT it; it is the patient’s legal responsibility to notify and stop, but per GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive (2017), if a patient continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded, the doctor should make every effort and then contact the DVLA promptly (telling the patient first and confirming in writing afterwards) — confidentiality yielding to public safety. The hidden agenda is fear for his livelihood plus minimisation; be empathetic about the job impact, fix adherence supportively, signpost work/practical support (fit note with amended duties; Access to Work travel funding), and be honest about the driving duty WITHOUT colluding.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG217 (epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022, updated January 2025) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: neurological disorders (epilepsy and seizures) and leaflet INS9 · [3] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017)
knowledge.summary: A breakthrough seizure in established epilepsy means he must stop driving now and tell the DVLA, whatever his tablets are doing. Explore why the doses were missed without blame, fix the supply problem, review control and safety, and support him through the loss of driving.

points.t: Ask openly: forgetting, running out, repeat prescription or pharmacy problems, feeling well and doubting the need, side-effects, cost or a chaotic routine. Missed or abruptly stopped anti-seizure medication can provoke seizures and, rarely, status epilepticus. NICE NG217 [1] supports adherence help such as simplified regimens, reminders and involving the pharmacist.

What happened, any injury or tongue biting, duration, recovery, other triggers (sleep loss, alcohol, illness, stress), other recent seizures including minor ones or auras. Consider an epilepsy specialist review (NICE NG217 [1]) if control was not truly established or the regimen needs change.

NICE NG217 [1]: discuss the individual risk of epilepsy-related death including SUDEP and how to reduce it; non-adherence to medication and uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures are modifiable risk factors. Everyday safety: showers not baths, care with heights, cooking and swimming alone, and a seizure plan for family or colleagues.

points.h: Driving: stop and tell the DVLA
points.t: DVLA [2]: after a seizure the driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Restarting medication does not change that. The law places the duty on the patient; the doctor advises clearly and records the advice.

DVLA Group 1 (car and motorcycle) [2]: epilepsy requires 12 months free of any seizure before relicensing (special rules cover asleep-only patterns and seizures without loss of consciousness). The 6-month period after a first unprovoked seizure does not apply to someone with established epilepsy. A shorter route after a seizure during medication change applies only when the change was made on medical advice. Group 2 (lorry and bus) requires 10 years seizure-free without medication. The DVLA makes the licensing decision.

GMC [3]: try to persuade him to stop and to notify. If he continues to drive against advice and you judge others are at risk of death or serious harm, contact the DVLA medical adviser promptly. Try to tell him before you disclose, and afterwards confirm in writing that you have done so; record it.
Explore the impact on his job. Access to Work can fund travel to work for people who cannot drive because of a health condition. A fit note can advise amended duties if non-driving work is possible.

dg.d: Open question; let him state his request about driving before steering; acknowledged his honesty about missed doses.
His work, long hours, finances, and how the loss of driving affects him.
Seizure description, injury, minor seizures, triggers, adherence reasons, mood.
Missed medication versus other triggers; whether control was truly established; need for specialist review.
Injury, recurrent or prolonged seizures, and safety at home; SUDEP information given sensitively.
Breakthrough seizure from missed medication in established epilepsy; DVLA Group 1 12-month rule.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop driving and notify the DVLA; adherence plan with pharmacy and reminders; epilepsy specialist review.
Work support (fit note amended duties, Access to Work) and mood.
999 for prolonged or clustered seizures; documented driving advice; review in four weeks; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “please don’t tell me I have to stop” and the work pressure behind the missed doses.
His idea (restarting tablets fixes it), concern (job and bills), and expectation (permission to drive).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — losing his job and income if he can't drive; embarrassed about letting his tablets lapse — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Lewis, I’m Dr Okafor. Thanks for getting in touch so quickly after last week. Tell me what happened.
model.why: Open question and acknowledges he sought help

model.text: So I had a seizure last week, first one in ages. I’ll be honest, I’d been missing my tablets. I got busy, ran out, felt fine, so I didn’t rush to sort it. I’m back on them now. I can carry on driving, can’t I? I drive for my job. Please don’t tell me I have to stop.

Thank you for being so honest about the tablets, that really helps. I can hear how much the driving matters, and we will talk about it properly, I promise. Can I first understand what happened, and then we’ll come to the car?
model.why: Acknowledges the agenda and sequences the consultation

model.text: Okay. Fair enough.
Talk me through the seizure. Where were you, was anyone with you, and were you hurt?
model.why: Reviews this seizure and screens for injury

model.text: At home. It was like my usual ones. I felt rough after, but I didn’t hurt myself as far as I know.
Good. Has there been anything else, even small ones, like the warning feelings or jerks you sometimes get, over the last few weeks?
model.why: Checks for other seizures, including minor ones

model.text: Not that I noticed.
And around that time, anything else going on: short of sleep, drinking more than usual, unwell, stressed?
Work’s been full on. Long days. That’s partly why I let the tablets slide.
Tell me about the tablets. Was it mainly running out, forgetting, or a sense that you didn’t really need them because you felt well? Any side-effects that put you off?
model.why: Explores the reasons for non-adherence without judgement

model.text: Running out, mostly. I kept meaning to order the repeat. And yeah, I felt fine, so it didn’t seem urgent.
That’s really common, and it’s fixable. The tablets work by keeping the level steady, so gaps, especially stopping suddenly, can bring seizures on. How are you in yourself with all this, your mood?
model.why: Explains why adherence matters; screens mood

model.text: Worried, if I’m honest. Mainly about work.
What’s the worry about work, exactly?
If I can’t drive, I don’t know how I keep my job. I’ve got bills. That’s why I’m hoping you’ll say restarting the tablets sorts it.
That’s a real worry, and I’m not going to brush past it. I also have to be straight with you, because it’s your safety and other people’s on the road.
model.why: Validates the livelihood fear before the hard message

model.text: After a seizure, the law says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA. Restarting the tablets is the right thing to do, but it doesn’t change that rule. I’m sorry, I know it’s the part you didn’t want to hear.
model.why: States the DVLA duty clearly and kindly

model.text: (silence) …For how long?

For a car licence, someone with epilepsy usually needs to be free of any seizures for 12 months before the DVLA will relicense. If you hold a lorry or bus licence as well, those rules are much stricter. The DVLA makes the final decision, but I’d plan on a year for a car.
model.why: Correct Group 1 rule for established epilepsy; mentions Group 2

model.text: A year. That’s… a lot.
It is. The good news is that taking the tablets every day is exactly what gets you back behind the wheel. Every month without a seizure counts toward it.
model.why: Frames adherence as the route back to driving

model.text: And if I just… kept quiet?

I understand why you’d ask. Driving after a seizure without telling the DVLA is illegal, your insurance wouldn’t cover you, and if you had a seizure at the wheel someone could be killed. It’s your legal responsibility to tell them. I’ll record today that I’ve advised you. If I learned that someone was still driving, I’d have to consider telling the DVLA myself, and I’d tell you first. I’d much rather help you do it.
model.why: Explains legal, insurance and GMC position honestly without threat

model.text: No, I get it. I don’t want to hurt anyone.

Let’s make the next year as manageable as we can. For the tablets: could the pharmacy send them automatically, and would phone reminders help? I can put a note on your repeat so it’s flagged before you run out.
The pharmacy thing would help. And alarms.

For work, is there part of your job that doesn’t involve driving? A fit note can suggest amended duties, and there’s a scheme called Access to Work that can pay towards travel to work when someone can’t drive for health reasons. It would be worth talking to your employer about it.
I didn’t know that existed. I’ll ask.

I’d also like the epilepsy team to review you, to make sure your treatment is right. And some safety points while things settle: showers rather than baths, no swimming alone, and care with heights. There’s also a rare risk of sudden death with poorly controlled epilepsy, and steady tablets are the best protection against it.
model.why: Specialist review, seizure safety and sensitive SUDEP information

model.text: Okay. That’s sobering.
If you have a seizure lasting more than five minutes, or one after another without coming round, whoever is with you should call 999. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do after this call?
Stop driving, tell the DVLA, sort the pharmacy and alarms, talk to work about Access to Work, and you’ll refer me to the epilepsy team.
That’s it exactly. I’ll see you in four weeks to see how the tablets and work are going. I know this is a hard day, and you’ve handled it well.

social.t: Losing a licence can threaten a job that involves driving. Explore alternative duties, travel options and finances; the fear is often what drives concealment.
The Access to Work scheme (DWP) can help pay for travel to work, such as taxis, for people who cannot use public transport or drive because of a health condition.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: after a seizure the driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Group 1 with epilepsy: 12 months free of any seizure before relicensing (asleep-only and no-loss-of-consciousness patterns have separate rules). Group 2: 10 years seizure-free without medication. Failing to notify can bring a fine of up to £1,000 and prosecution if involved in a collision.
Driving without meeting the medical standards, or without declaring the condition, is likely to invalidate motor insurance.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive (2017): make sure the patient understands the condition may affect driving and that they have a legal duty to tell the DVLA. If they continue to drive and put others at risk of death or serious harm, contact the DVLA promptly; try to tell the patient first and confirm in writing afterwards. Record the advice given.
A fit note can state “may be fit for work” with amended duties (no driving) where the employer can accommodate it.

community.t: Epilepsy Action and the Epilepsy Society offer information on driving, work and SUDEP. The community pharmacy can set up managed repeat dispensing or collection reminders.

redFlags: Prolonged seizure or clusters without recovery (status epilepticus risk)
Head injury, tongue biting or other injury during the seizure
Other recent seizures, including minor ones, suggesting control was not established
Low mood or hopelessness about work and driving
psychosocial: Job that involves driving and the financial pressure behind his request
Long working hours and sleep loss as triggers
ice: Idea: restarting the tablets means he is safe to drive
Concern: losing his job and not paying the bills

playbook.diagnosis: “This was a breakthrough seizure, almost certainly because of the gap in your tablets. Because you have epilepsy, the law says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA, and for a car licence you’ll usually need 12 months without any seizures before you can drive again.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your tablets are like a dam holding back the water. When the level drops because doses are missed, the water can spill over. Once it has spilled, the DVLA wants to see the dam hold for a full year before you drive again.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened about your job and the bills, and that’s exactly why I want to help you plan the next year, not just tell you to stop.”
management.psychosocial: Pair the hard message with real help: Access to Work for travel, amended duties via a fit note, and a conversation with his employer. Check his mood again at review.
sharedPlan: Stop driving now and notify the DVLA (his legal duty); advice documented
Adherence: pharmacy repeat system, phone reminders, flag on the repeat record
safetyNet: 999 if a seizure lasts over five minutes or seizures follow one another without recovery
Review in four weeks; sooner if further seizures or low mood

pitfalls.intro: The clinical part of this station is straightforward. It is failed on driving: either colluding with a frightened man, or delivering the DVLA rule as a threat with no help attached.

items.fail: Quoting “six months off driving” because that is the first-seizure rule.
items.why: He has established epilepsy. The Group 1 rule is 12 months seizure-free. Wrong rules are a clinical management fail.
items.fix: “For someone with epilepsy, it’s usually 12 months without any seizure for a car licence. The DVLA decides.”

items.fail: Letting him think restarting the tablets means he can drive.
items.why: Collusion with unsafe driving; also misses the legal and insurance consequences.
items.fix: “Restarting them is right, and it’s how you get back to driving, but the law says stop now and tell the DVLA.”

items.fail: Never asking why the tablets were missed.
items.why: The cause (running out, feeling well) is the thing to fix; without it the seizure will recur.
items.fix: “Was it running out, forgetting, or feeling you didn’t need them?” Then a practical plan with the pharmacy.

items.fail: Telling him off for stopping his medication.
items.why: “Judgemental approach.” He was honest; blame makes concealment more likely next time.
items.fix: Thank him for his honesty and normalise the problem before solving it.

items.fail: Delivering the driving rule and moving on without acknowledging his job.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” The livelihood fear is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Name the fear, then bring concrete help: Access to Work, amended duties, talking to his employer.

items.fail: No documentation of the driving advice and no plan if he keeps driving.
items.why: The GMC expects the advice recorded and a clear, honest route if he does not comply.
items.fix: “I’m recording that I’ve advised you. If someone kept driving I’d have to consider telling the DVLA, and I’d tell you first.”

timeMap.d: He puts the driving question first. Acknowledge it and promise to return to it; do not answer before you know what happened.
Description, injury, minor seizures, triggers, reasons for missed doses, mood. No blame.
The fear for his job and bills. Validate it before the hard message.
Stop now, tell the DVLA, 12 months seizure-free for a car in established epilepsy, Group 2 far stricter. Legal, insurance and GMC position without threat.
Pharmacy and reminders, work support, specialist review, safety and SUDEP, 999 advice, teach-back, review in four weeks.

wordPics.fail: Tells him he can drive now he is back on tablets, or quotes the 6-month first-seizure rule; lectures him about non-adherence; never asks why doses were missed; no DVLA advice documented; ignores the job worry.
wordPics.pass: Explores adherence without blame, reviews the seizure, states clearly that he must stop driving and tell the DVLA, knows the 12-month Group 1 rule, and gives a basic adherence and safety plan.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: validates the livelihood fear before the hard news and returns to it with concrete help (Access to Work, amended duties); frames adherence as the route back to driving; handles “what if I keep quiet?” honestly with the GMC position; gives SUDEP information sensitively; teach-back and booked review.

avoid.dont: “Now you’re back on your tablets you should be fine to drive.”
avoid.instead: “Restarting them is right, but the law still says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA.”
avoid.why: Colluding with continued driving is unsafe and a professional failure.

avoid.dont: “You shouldn’t have stopped your tablets. This is what happens.”
avoid.instead: “Running out when life’s busy is really common. Let’s set up a system so it doesn’t happen again.”
avoid.why: Blame shuts down the adherence conversation and damages the relationship.

avoid.dont: “If you drive I’ll report you to the DVLA.”
avoid.instead: “It’s your responsibility to tell them. If someone kept driving I’d have to consider telling them myself, and I’d tell you first. I’d rather help you do it.”
avoid.why: A threat destroys trust; an honest explanation of the GMC position keeps him on side.

SCA_MODELS.text: (silence) …For how long?

For a car licence, someone with epilepsy usually needs to be free of any seizures for 12 months before the DVLA will relicense. If you hold a lorry or bus licence as well, those rules are much stricter. The DVLA makes the final decision, but I’d plan on a year for a car.
SCA_MODELS.why: Correct Group 1 rule for established epilepsy; mentions Group 2

SCA_MODELS.text: A year. That’s… a lot.
It is. The good news is that taking the tablets every day is exactly what gets you back behind the wheel. Every month without a seizure counts toward it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frames adherence as the route back to driving

SCA_MODELS.text: And if I just… kept quiet?

I understand why you’d ask. Driving after a seizure without telling the DVLA is illegal, your insurance wouldn’t cover you, and if you had a seizure at the wheel someone could be killed. It’s your legal responsibility to tell them. I’ll record today that I’ve advised you. If I learned that someone was still driving, I’d have to consider telling the DVLA myself, and I’d tell you first. I’d much rather help you do it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains legal, insurance and GMC position honestly without threat

SCA_MODELS.text: No, I get it. I don’t want to hurt anyone.

Let’s make the next year as manageable as we can. For the tablets: could the pharmacy send them automatically, and would phone reminders help? I can put a note on your repeat so it’s flagged before you run out.
The pharmacy thing would help. And alarms.

For work, is there part of your job that doesn’t involve driving? A fit note can suggest amended duties, and there’s a scheme called Access to Work that can pay towards travel to work when someone can’t drive for health reasons. It would be worth talking to your employer about it.
I didn’t know that existed. I’ll ask.

I’d also like the epilepsy team to review you, to make sure your treatment is right. And some safety points while things settle: showers rather than baths, no swimming alone, and care with heights. There’s also a rare risk of sudden death with poorly controlled epilepsy, and steady tablets are the best protection against it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specialist review, seizure safety and sensitive SUDEP information

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s sobering.
If you have a seizure lasting more than five minutes, or one after another without coming round, whoever is with you should call 999. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do after this call?
Stop driving, tell the DVLA, sort the pharmacy and alarms, talk to work about Access to Work, and you’ll refer me to the epilepsy team.
That’s it exactly. I’ll see you in four weeks to see how the tablets and work are going. I know this is a hard day, and you’ve handled it well.

SCA_STEM.name: Lewis Tran
meds: Anti-seizure medication (as on the repeat record); recent gap in collection
SCA_STEM.recent: Breakthrough seizure last week after a period of missed medication. Has since restarted his tablets.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “I’ve restarted my tablets. I can keep driving, can’t I? I need my car for work.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG217 (epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022, updated January 2025) · [2] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: neurological disorders (epilepsy and seizures) and leaflet INS9 · [3] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A breakthrough seizure in established epilepsy means he must stop driving now and tell the DVLA, whatever his tablets are doing. Explore why the doses were missed without blame, fix the supply problem, review control and safety, and support him through the loss of driving.

points.t: Ask openly: forgetting, running out, repeat prescription or pharmacy problems, feeling well and doubting the need, side-effects, cost or a chaotic routine. Missed or abruptly stopped anti-seizure medication can provoke seizures and, rarely, status epilepticus. NICE NG217 [1] supports adherence help such as simplified regimens, reminders and involving the pharmacist.

What happened, any injury or tongue biting, duration, recovery, other triggers (sleep loss, alcohol, illness, stress), other recent seizures including minor ones or auras. Consider an epilepsy specialist review (NICE NG217 [1]) if control was not truly established or the regimen needs change.

NICE NG217 [1]: discuss the individual risk of epilepsy-related death including SUDEP and how to reduce it; non-adherence to medication and uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures are modifiable risk factors. Everyday safety: showers not baths, care with heights, cooking and swimming alone, and a seizure plan for family or colleagues.

points.h: Driving: stop and tell the DVLA
points.t: DVLA [2]: after a seizure the driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Restarting medication does not change that. The law places the duty on the patient; the doctor advises clearly and records the advice.

DVLA Group 1 (car and motorcycle) [2]: epilepsy requires 12 months free of any seizure before relicensing (special rules cover asleep-only patterns and seizures without loss of consciousness). The 6-month period after a first unprovoked seizure does not apply to someone with established epilepsy. A shorter route after a seizure during medication change applies only when the change was made on medical advice. Group 2 (lorry and bus) requires 10 years seizure-free without medication. The DVLA makes the licensing decision.

GMC [3]: try to persuade him to stop and to notify. If he continues to drive against advice and you judge others are at risk of death or serious harm, contact the DVLA medical adviser promptly. Try to tell him before you disclose, and afterwards confirm in writing that you have done so; record it.
Explore the impact on his job. Access to Work can fund travel to work for people who cannot drive because of a health condition. A fit note can advise amended duties if non-driving work is possible.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him state his request about driving before steering; acknowledged his honesty about missed doses.
His work, long hours, finances, and how the loss of driving affects him.
Picked up “please don’t tell me I have to stop” and the work pressure behind the missed doses.
His idea (restarting tablets fixes it), concern (job and bills), and expectation (permission to drive).
Seizure description, injury, minor seizures, triggers, adherence reasons, mood.
Missed medication versus other triggers; whether control was truly established; need for specialist review.
Injury, recurrent or prolonged seizures, and safety at home; SUDEP information given sensitively.
Breakthrough seizure from missed medication in established epilepsy; DVLA Group 1 12-month rule.
Stop driving and notify the DVLA; adherence plan with pharmacy and reminders; epilepsy specialist review.
Work support (fit note amended duties, Access to Work) and mood.
999 for prolonged or clustered seizures; documented driving advice; review in four weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Losing a licence can threaten a job that involves driving. Explore alternative duties, travel options and finances; the fear is often what drives concealment.
The Access to Work scheme (DWP) can help pay for travel to work, such as taxis, for people who cannot use public transport or drive because of a health condition.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: after a seizure the driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA. Group 1 with epilepsy: 12 months free of any seizure before relicensing (asleep-only and no-loss-of-consciousness patterns have separate rules). Group 2: 10 years seizure-free without medication. Failing to notify can bring a fine of up to £1,000 and prosecution if involved in a collision.
Driving without meeting the medical standards, or without declaring the condition, is likely to invalidate motor insurance.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive (2017): make sure the patient understands the condition may affect driving and that they have a legal duty to tell the DVLA. If they continue to drive and put others at risk of death or serious harm, contact the DVLA promptly; try to tell the patient first and confirm in writing afterwards. Record the advice given.
A fit note can state “may be fit for work” with amended duties (no driving) where the employer can accommodate it.

community.t: Epilepsy Action and the Epilepsy Society offer information on driving, work and SUDEP. The community pharmacy can set up managed repeat dispensing or collection reminders.

redFlags: Prolonged seizure or clusters without recovery (status epilepticus risk)
Head injury, tongue biting or other injury during the seizure
Other recent seizures, including minor ones, suggesting control was not established
Low mood or hopelessness about work and driving
psychosocial: Job that involves driving and the financial pressure behind his request
Long working hours and sleep loss as triggers
ice: Idea: restarting the tablets means he is safe to drive
Concern: losing his job and not paying the bills

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This was a breakthrough seizure, almost certainly because of the gap in your tablets. Because you have epilepsy, the law says you must stop driving and tell the DVLA, and for a car licence you’ll usually need 12 months without any seizures before you can drive again.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your tablets are like a dam holding back the water. When the level drops because doses are missed, the water can spill over. Once it has spilled, the DVLA wants to see the dam hold for a full year before you drive again.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened about your job and the bills, and that’s exactly why I want to help you plan the next year, not just tell you to stop.”
management.psychosocial: Pair the hard message with real help: Access to Work for travel, amended duties via a fit note, and a conversation with his employer. Check his mood again at review.
sharedPlan: Stop driving now and notify the DVLA (his legal duty); advice documented
Adherence: pharmacy repeat system, phone reminders, flag on the repeat record
safetyNet: 999 if a seizure lasts over five minutes or seizures follow one another without recovery
Review in four weeks; sooner if further seizures or low mood

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical part of this station is straightforward. It is failed on driving: either colluding with a frightened man, or delivering the DVLA rule as a threat with no help attached.

items.fail: Quoting “six months off driving” because that is the first-seizure rule.
items.why: He has established epilepsy. The Group 1 rule is 12 months seizure-free. Wrong rules are a clinical management fail.
items.fix: “For someone with epilepsy, it’s usually 12 months without any seizure for a car licence. The DVLA decides.”

items.fail: Letting him think restarting the tablets means he can drive.
items.why: Collusion with unsafe driving; also misses the legal and insurance consequences.
items.fix: “Restarting them is right, and it’s how you get back to driving, but the law says stop now and tell the DVLA.”

items.fail: Never asking why the tablets were missed.
items.why: The cause (running out, feeling well) is the thing to fix; without it the seizure will recur.
items.fix: “Was it running out, forgetting, or feeling you didn’t need them?” Then a practical plan with the pharmacy.

items.fail: Telling him off for stopping his medication.
items.why: “Judgemental approach.” He was honest; blame makes concealment more likely next time.
items.fix: Thank him for his honesty and normalise the problem before solving it.

items.fail: Delivering the driving rule and moving on without acknowledging his job.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” The livelihood fear is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Name the fear, then bring concrete help: Access to Work, amended duties, talking to his employer.

items.fail: No documentation of the driving advice and no plan if he keeps driving.
items.why: The GMC expects the advice recorded and a clear, honest route if he does not comply.
items.fix: “I’m recording that I’ve advised you. If someone kept driving I’d have to consider telling the DVLA, and I’d tell you first.”
